hints: Focus on counting electrons, not atoms. Remember a negative ion has extra electrons compared to its neutral atoms.
Oxygen brings 8 electrons and hydrogen brings 1, then add one more for the 1- charge to get the total for $\text{OH}^-$.
Now look for the neutral atom whose atomic number matches that total, since a neutral atom has electrons equal to protons.
walkthrough:
**Count the electrons in OH-**

Think of $\text{OH}^-$ as O plus H plus the extra charge. Oxygen has atomic number 8, so 8 electrons, and hydrogen has 1 electron.

Total calculation:
$$8 \text{ (from O)} + 1 \text{ (from H)} + 1 \text{ (from - charge)} = 10 \text{ electrons}$$

**Count the electrons in the neutral atoms**

For a neutral atom, electrons = protons = atomic number. So F has 9, Ne has 10, Na has 11, and Mg has 12 electrons.

**Match them up**

Only one atom has exactly 10 electrons, the same as $\text{OH}^-$. That is the isoelectronic match you are looking for.

options.A: F has atomic number 9, so a neutral F atom has 9 electrons. That is one short of the 10 electrons in OH-, a common slip if you forget to add the extra electron for the negative charge.
options.B: Ne has atomic number 10, so a neutral Ne atom has 10 electrons. This exactly matches the 10 electrons in OH-, so they are isoelectronic.
options.C: Na has atomic number 11, so a neutral Na atom has 11 electrons. That is one too many, chosen if you miscount the charge or confuse Na atom with Na+ ion which would have 10.
options.D: Mg has atomic number 12, so a neutral Mg atom has 12 electrons. That is two too many, chosen if you confuse Mg atom with Mg2+ ion which would have 10.
